This character is adheres to the School of Saint Mark. This school draws on the ancient and esteemed School of Alexandria in its teachings. This school relied on metaphorical exegesis of Sacred Scripture and was valued throughout Christendom.

This character adheres to the School of Saint Peter. This school originates from the ancient School of Antioch, which, unlike the School of Alexandria, favored a literal interpretation of Holy Scripture and a full experience of the person of Jesus Christ. Representatives of this school possess a strong diplomatic and medical aptitude.

This character is in keeping with the School of Saint Mathew. This school has its roots firmly planted in Ethiopia, a Christian country that Apostolic Christians prided itself on serving. For this reason, representatives of this school emphasize service to the state and good stewardship of the common good.

This character adheres to the School of Saint Thaddeus. This school was born in Persian and Syrian territories hostile to Christianity. Christians there lived under constant threat and had to constantly defend their lives and the lives of their fellow believers.

In Feudalism, the Church is not linked to the realm as in cenobitism or monastic rule. They are separate, and the property and rights of the Church are distinct from those of the realm. Clergy also do not dominate state government, although they support it with counsel and prayer.

Although Monastic Feudalism maintains a distinction between clerical and secular authority, it significantly increases the role of clergy, particularly monks, in governing the realm. Law and administration in such a realm are steeped in religion and religious principles.

In Transitional Monastic Feudalism, a slow transformation from cenobitism to monastic feudalism or vice versa takes place. Authority is more spiritualized, and the church community is more integrated with the government than in monasticism, but it does not have all the features of cenobitic government.
In the Cenobitic Government, there is no longer much distinction between religious and political communities. Power in the realm rests with celibate and non-celibate clergy.

In Pachomial Cenobitism, there is no distinction between the religious and political communities. Authority rests with celibate clergy who devote all their energies to caring for the common good, both spiritual and temporal.

Based on the concept of a commonwealth of believers, cenobitic government is governed by theocratic councils in league with elected elders. This style of government favors the clergy as being competent not only to teach but also to exercise dominion over the faithful and causes the state to be absorbed by the religion.
These laws have consequences in defining the relationship between realm and church, and precisely how far the distinction between one and the other is.
